title: Hollywood and ByteDance Strike Deal on AI Copyright Protections
excerpt: The agreement covers ByteDance's Seedance and Seedream AI models, resolving a six-month standoff over unauthorized generation of copyrighted characters and celebrity likenesses.
body:
• ByteDance and the Motion Picture Association signed an agreement Monday to strengthen copyright safeguards on ByteDance's Seedance video and Seedream image-generation AI models.
  • The deal resolves a standoff that began in February when Disney and other major studios sent cease-and-desist letters over unauthorized generation of copyrighted characters and celebrity likenesses.
  • The AI models are offered through TikTok, CapCut, and Dreamina, and ByteDance says newer versions include stronger IP protections.
  • Both sides committed to ongoing collaboration on safeguards as generative AI technology evolves.

ByteDance and the Motion Picture Association on Monday signed an agreement to strengthen copyright protections on the Chinese company's AI-powered video and image-generation tools, resolving a six-month standoff that saw Hollywood studios accuse the TikTok parent of "massive scale" intellectual property infringement.

The deal covers ByteDance's Seedance video-generation model and Seedream image-generation model, both of which are available through services including TikTok, CapCut, and Dreamina. ByteDance said newer versions of the models include stronger intellectual property safeguards, and both parties committed to continued collaboration as the technology evolves, according to Reuters.

From Cease-and-Desist to Cooperation

The agreement follows months of escalating tension between Hollywood and ByteDance. When Seedance 2.0 launched on February 12, users quickly demonstrated that the tool could generate realistic video clips featuring copyrighted characters from Disney, Marvel, and other major franchises, as well as likenesses of Hollywood actors — all without authorization.

https://x.com/nypost/status/2089415030626189465

The MPA, which represents Disney, Sony, Universal, Netflix, Paramount, Warner Bros. Discovery, and Amazon's MGM, issued an immediate public rebuke. Within days, six of its seven member studios had sent individual cease-and-desist letters to ByteDance's Culver City, California, office.

"By launching a service that operates without meaningful safeguards against infringement, ByteDance is disregarding well-established copyright law that protects the rights of creators and underpins millions of American jobs."

— Charles Rivkin, Chairman and CEO, Motion Picture Association

The Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists also condemned the tool, and Japan's government contacted ByteDance to demand adjustments. ByteDance responded by temporarily halting Seedance 2.0's ability to generate realistic human faces and IP-protected characters.

What the Deal Means

The specific terms of Monday's agreement were not publicly disclosed, but the MPA's decision to sign a cooperative pact rather than pursue litigation suggests ByteDance has implemented safeguards that the studios consider meaningful — or at least sufficient as a starting point.

The deal stands in contrast to the approach taken by other AI companies. Disney struck a licensing agreement with OpenAI in December 2025 that allows the Sora video model to use more than 200 Disney characters, with Disney taking a stake in OpenAI and investing $1 billion. Meanwhile, Disney, Universal, and Warner Bros. Discovery have sued AI image-generator developers Midjourney and MiniMax over alleged IP infringement.

The ByteDance agreement appears to fall somewhere between those extremes — not a paid licensing arrangement, but a set of agreed-upon guardrails rather than open legal warfare.

The Broader AI Copyright Landscape

Monday's deal arrives amid a global reckoning over how AI companies use copyrighted material. Studios, authors, musicians, and visual artists have filed lawsuits against multiple AI developers, arguing that training models on protected works without permission constitutes infringement. AI companies have generally countered that such use qualifies as fair use.

For ByteDance, the agreement removes a legal overhang that had threatened its AI ambitions in Western markets. For Hollywood, it establishes a precedent that AI companies can be pressured into implementing copyright safeguards through collective industry action — without necessarily going to court.

Both sides acknowledged that the arrangement will need to evolve. Generative AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, and the safeguards that work today may prove inadequate as models become more powerful. The commitment to ongoing collaboration suggests neither party views Monday's deal as a final resolution.
